doc.title: Geometric Deep Learning Grids, Groups, Graphs, Geodesics, and Gauges

proposal.title: Geometric Deep Learning Grids, Groups, Graphs, Geodesics, and Gauges
proposal.gist: Geometric Deep Learning unifies CNNs, GNNs, and related architectures by deriving them from symmetry and invariance principles applied to underlying domains.
proposal.question: Deep learning architectures — why do so many different neural networks succeed, and can they be unified? (a blueprint built from symmetry principles)

children.title: Preface
children.gist: Following Felix Klein's Erlangen Programme, which defined geometries by their symmetry groups, this text applies the same symmetry-first logic to unify deep learning architectures.
children.question: Deep learning architectures — can the chaos of neural network designs be organized the way Klein organized geometry? (a historical analogy)

children.title: Notation
children.gist: A reference table defines the mathematical symbols used throughout for domains, signals, groups, and geometric operators.

children.title: Introduction
children.gist: Deep learning succeeds on high-dimensional tasks because architectures exploit low-dimensional geometric regularities and symmetries of the data's domain, a unifying lens the authors call Geometric Deep Learning.
children.question: Deep learning's success — why do neural networks beat the curse of dimensionality on real tasks? (a unifying principle: geometric symmetry)

children.title: Learning in High Dimensions
children.gist: Generic high-dimensional function learning is cursed by exponentially many samples needed, so some additional structural assumption beyond smoothness is required to make learning feasible.
children.question: High-dimensional learning — why does the curse of dimensionality make generic interpolation hopeless, and what kind of prior could fix it? (an argument from sample complexity)

children.title: Supervised Learning Setup
children.gist: Supervised learning is framed as estimating an unknown function from high-dimensional data to labels using a parametrised function class, with performance judged by expected loss on new samples.

children.title: Inductive Bias via Function Regularity
children.gist: Even though neural networks can approximate almost any function, learning still relies on an inductive bias, since one seeks the simplest function fitting the data as measured by some complexity norm, borrowing ideas from splines and Banach spaces.

children.title: The Curse of Dimensionality
children.gist: Unlike low-dimensional interpolation, learning a merely smooth (Lipschitz or Sobolev) function in high dimensions requires exponentially many samples in the dimension, and sparsity-based tricks only escape this curse under unrealistic assumptions, motivating the search for geometric regularity instead.

children.title: Geometric Priors
children.gist: Two principles — symmetry of the domain and scale separation across it — let models beat the curse of dimensionality, and together they yield a general blueprint combining equivariant local maps, invariant global pooling, and coarsening.
children.question: Geometric priors — how do symmetry and scale separation combine into one construction recipe for stable, expressive architectures? (a blueprint of four building blocks)

children.title: Two Geometric Priors
children.gist: Beyond smoothness, physically-structured data can exploit symmetry and scale separation, treating inputs as signals forming a Hilbert space on an underlying domain, which lets architectures like CNNs beat the curse of dimensionality.

children.title: Symmetries, Representations, and Invariance
children.gist: Symmetries form groups that act on domains and, via representations, on signals, and this structure lets functions be classified as invariant (unchanged by the action) or equivariant (transformed consistently with it).

children.title: Isomorphisms and Automorphisms
children.gist: Different levels of structure on a domain (set, topology, metric, manifold) yield different symmetry groups via subgroups, and automorphisms (self-equivalences) must be distinguished from isomorphisms (equivalences between distinct objects).

children.title: Deformation Stability
children.gist: Because exact symmetry groups fail to capture real-world noise, deformation stability relaxes invariance into a quantitative bound using a deformation cost, applied separately to signal deformations and to deformations of the domain itself.

children.title: Scale Separation
children.gist: Because global Fourier representations are unstable under small deformations, multiscale wavelet-like decompositions that are localised in both space and frequency offer stable features, motivating a scale separation prior that factors functions through domain coarsening.

children.title: The Blueprint of Geometric Deep Learning
children.gist: Combining symmetry, stability, and scale separation yields a universal blueprint of four building blocks — local equivariant maps, nonlinearities, coarsening, and global invariant pooling — composed to build any G-invariant deep learning architecture.
children.sourceHeading: 3.5 The Blueprint of Geometric Deep Learning

children.title: Geometric Domains: the 5 Gs
children.gist: Grids, graphs, groups, geodesics (manifolds), and gauges are five kinds of structured domains, each carrying its own symmetry group, on which the geometric blueprint's convolution and invariance ideas can be instantiated concretely.
children.question: The five geometric domains — what symmetry group and convolution operation fits each of grids, graphs, groups, manifolds, and gauge bundles? (five worked constructions)

children.title: Introducing the Five Domains
children.gist: Graphs, grids, groups, geodesics (manifolds), and gauges are the five structured domains the text will use to instantiate the geometric blueprint's convolution and invariance ideas, chosen for concept-building rather than strict generality.

children.title: 4.1 Graphs and Sets
children.gist: Because a graph's nodes have no fixed order, valid functions on graphs must be permutation invariant or equivariant, and a local neighbourhood-aggregation recipe built from an invariant function gives a general way to construct such equivariant functions.

children.title: 4.2 Grids and Euclidean spaces
children.gist: Grids are graphs with fixed node order, which replaces permutation invariance with translation invariance, and this symmetry alone forces linear equivariant operators to be convolutions whose eigenbasis is exactly the Fourier transform.

children.title: 4.3 Groups and Homogeneous spaces
children.gist: Convolution and the Fourier transform generalise beyond translations to any locally compact symmetry group acting on a homogeneous domain, as shown through group convolution and worked examples like cyclic shifts and spherical rotations.

children.title: 4.4 Geodesics and Manifolds
children.gist: Manifolds generally lack a global symmetry group, so invariance must instead come from intrinsic, metric-based quantities such as geodesic distance, parallel transport, and the Laplacian, yielding isometry-invariant spectral and spatial convolutions.

children.title: 4.5 Gauges and Bundles
children.gist: A gauge is a local reference frame for a vector bundle's fibres, such as the tangent bundle, and because this choice is arbitrary, functions on manifolds must be built to stay equivariant under changes of gauge via the bundle's structure group.

children.title: 4.6 Geometric graphs and Meshes
children.gist: Meshes sit between graphs and manifolds, letting the cotangent Laplacian give an intrinsic, isometry-invariant discretisation of manifold convolution that extends to functional maps allowing comparison across differently-discretised meshes.

children.title: Geometric Deep Learning Models
children.gist: CNNs, group-equivariant CNNs, GNNs, Deep Sets/Transformers, equivariant message passing, intrinsic mesh CNNs, and RNNs/LSTMs can each be derived as instances of the blueprint applied to a specific domain and symmetry group.
children.question: Popular architectures — how does each major neural network design (CNN, GNN, Transformer, RNN, LSTM...) fall out of the same symmetry blueprint? (seven worked derivations)

children.title: Overview of model derivations
children.gist: This chapter previews how CNNs, group-equivariant CNNs, GNNs, Deep Sets, Transformers, equivariant message passing, mesh CNNs and RNNs all follow from the same geometric blueprint applied to different domains.

children.title: Convolutional Neural Networks
children.gist: CNNs realize the translation-equivariant local linear operator as ordinary convolution, expressible as a weighted sum of shifted filter generators acting on grid signals, extended to multiple input and output channels.

children.title: Efficient multiscale computation
children.gist: A non-linearity like ReLU followed by grid coarsening (pooling) lets stacked convolutional layers build multiscale filters with growing receptive fields but constant parameter count per scale, yielding the vanilla CNN layer.

children.title: Deep and Residual Networks
children.gist: Deeper but thinner CNNs tend to work better empirically, and ResNets improve on this by reparametrizing each layer as a small perturbation of the input, equivalent to discretizing a continuous dynamical system that is easier to optimize.

children.title: Normalisation
children.gist: Borrowed from theories of neural gain control, normalisation layers such as batch normalisation rescale activations using local mean and variance statistics, boosting CNN performance though a full theoretical explanation remains elusive.

children.title: Data augmentation
children.gist: Because CNNs only encode translation and scale symmetries, practitioners add other known invariances like lighting or rotation by augmenting training data with transformed copies, though this is provably less sample-efficient than building the symmetry into the architecture.

children.title: Group-equivariant CNNs
children.gist: Convolution generalises from Euclidean grids to any homogeneous space by moving a filter around the domain using a transitive group action, such as rotating as well as translating it, giving group convolution.

children.title: Discrete group convolution
children.gist: Discrete rotation-translation symmetry on 3D medical scans and the reverse-complement symmetry of DNA strands both illustrate group convolution, computed as an inner product between a signal and a group-transformed filter.

children.title: Transform+Convolve approach
children.gist: Group convolution can be computed efficiently in two steps — transforming (e.g. rotating) a base filter into several copies, then running ordinary translational convolution with each — yielding stacked orientation channels that permute equivariantly under the group.

children.title: Spherical CNNs in the Fourier domain
children.gist: For the continuous sphere symmetry group, convolution can be implemented spectrally using spherical harmonics and Wigner D-functions as Fourier bases, with fast transform algorithms making multi-layer spherical CNNs efficient.

children.title: Graph Neural Networks
children.gist: GNNs implement permutation equivariance on graphs via a shared local function over neighbourhoods, and nearly all published GNN layers fall into three flavours — convolutional, attentional, and message-passing — each trading expressiveness for cost, with convolutional contained in attentional contained in message-passing.

children.title: Deep Sets, Transformers, and Latent Graph Inference
children.gist: Sets lack given adjacency or ordering, so permutation-equivariant architectures for them arise by choosing how much interaction between elements to model, ranging from none to complete to learned.

children.title: Empty edge set
children.gist: Treating each set element independently, with no assumed edges, gives a shared per-element transformation equivalent to a convolutional GNN with self-loops only, known as Deep Sets or, for point clouds, PointNets.

children.title: Complete edge set
children.gist: Assuming every pair of elements is connected, convolutional aggregation collapses to a useless constant, but switching to the attentional GNN flavour recovers self-attention, making Transformers exactly attentional GNNs over a complete graph that need positional encodings to recover sequence order; learning the adjacency matrix itself, called latent graph inference, is a harder, still-open middle ground between these extremes.

children.title: Equivariant Message Passing Networks
children.gist: When node features include 3D spatial coordinates, as in molecules, a GNN layer can be made equivariant to rigid motions by updating coordinates only through pairwise distances, as shown in Satorras et al.'s equivariant message passing model.

children.title: Irreducible representations
children.gist: One family of equivariant layers decomposes roto-translation symmetry into irreducible blocks governed by Wigner D-matrices, with equivariant kernels found by solving linear constraints, as used in Tensor Field Networks, 3D Steerable CNNs, and the SE(3)-Transformer.

children.title: Regular representations
children.gist: An alternative, more general but costlier approach stores feature copies for every group element, exemplified by Lie-group methods like LieConv and LieTransformer that use exponential and logarithmic maps for rapid prototyping across symmetry groups.

children.title: Intrinsic Mesh CNNs
children.gist: Triangular meshes, the standard representation for 3D objects in computer graphics, motivated adapting CNN-style convolution to surfaces by discretising or approximating the exponential map in a local tangent coordinate system.

children.title: Geodesic patches
children.gist: A geodesic patch defines local polar coordinates of distance and angle around a mesh point by shooting geodesics outward, computed via the Fast Marching algorithm, forming the basis of the first intrinsic mesh CNN, Masci et al.'s Geodesic CNN.

children.title: Isotropic filters
children.gist: Because the reference direction used to define a geodesic patch is arbitrary (a gauge ambiguity), one simple fix is to use direction-independent isotropic filters, as spectral Laplacian-based methods do, though this discards useful directional edge information.

children.title: Fixed gauge
children.gist: Another fix is to pick a fixed gauge, such as Monti et al.'s principal curvature directions (reasonable for deformable but not flat or uniformly curved shapes) or later intrinsic gradient-based constructions that are robust to noise and remeshing.

children.title: Angular pooling
children.gist: Masci et al.'s angular max pooling keeps a directional filter but matches it against the patch at every possible rotation and keeps the strongest response, discretised on meshes via learnable or fixed weighting functions called patch operators.

children.title: Gauge-equivariant filters
children.gist: Rather than discarding directional information for gauge invariance, features can instead transform according to a chosen group representation under gauge changes, implemented on meshes as a message-passing convolution with parallel-transport and angle-dependent filter matrices satisfying linear equivariance constraints.

children.title: Recurrent Neural Networks
children.gist: For sequential inputs like video, text or traffic data on a fixed domain, an encoder respecting the domain's symmetry first produces per-step representations, which a recurrent neural network then aggregates respecting the temporal order of arrival.

children.title: SimpleRNNs
children.gist: The basic SimpleRNN computes a summary vector at each step as a single fully-connected layer combining the current input and previous summary, trained by unrolling the recurrence and applying backpropagation through time.

children.title: Translation equivariance in RNNs
children.gist: RNNs are not trivially translation equivariant over time, but with left-padding and an initial summary chosen as a fixed point of the update function (guaranteed by making it a contraction), shift equivariance can be recovered, though the resulting depth equal to sequence length causes vanishing or exploding gradients that gating mechanisms were invented to address.

children.title: Long Short-Term Memory networks
children.gist: The LSTM adds a memory cell preserved across steps and three learned gating vectors (input, forget, output) that control how much new information enters, how much old state is kept, and how much is exposed, mitigating vanishing gradients.

children.title: Time warping invariance of gated RNNs
children.gist: Analysing RNNs as continuous-time dynamical systems shows that invariance to time warping (resampling the input at a changing rate) requires an update rule with a learnable gate approximating the warping derivative, exactly the form of LSTM gates, explaining why gating helps model long-range dependencies and motivating chrono initialisation of the forget bias.

children.title: Sequence-to-sequence learning with RNNs
children.gist: Early seq2seq translation models compressed an entire input sequence into one fixed bottleneck summary vector, a limitation later eased by recurrent attention over all encoder states and further by pointer networks and the set2set architecture for unordered inputs.

children.title: Problems and Applications
children.gist: Across chemistry, biology, recommendation, traffic, vision, games, language, healthcare, physics, and graphics, real-world problems are already being solved by matching their natural domain's symmetry to a Geometric Deep Learning architecture.
children.question: Real-world impact — in which fields has matching data to its natural symmetry group already paid off? (a survey of domains and case studies)

children.title: Overview of Applications
children.gist: Geometric Deep Learning has quietly powered many of the 21st century's most popular machine-learning successes, and this chapter surveys influential examples across science and industry to motivate further study.

children.title: Chemistry and Drug Design
children.gist: Graph neural networks accelerate drug discovery by screening the vast space of possible molecules computationally, as shown when Stokes et al. used a GNN to find the antibiotic Halicin among repurposed compounds.

children.title: Drug Repositioning
children.gist: Modeling biochemical interactions as graphs lets Geometric Deep Learning support drug repositioning, reusing approved drugs for new purposes, as in Zitnik et al.'s prediction of polypharmacy side effects and COVID-19 related efforts.

children.title: Protein Biology
children.gist: Representing proteins as graphs or 3D meshes enables prediction of structure, function, and interactions, exemplified by AlphaFold's contact graphs and MaSIF's mesh-based design of cancer immunotherapy proteins.

children.title: Recommender Systems and Social Networks
children.gist: Large-scale graph representation learning now drives recommender systems like Pinterest's PinSage and detects misinformation spread on social networks, as in the Fabula AI system acquired by Twitter.

children.title: Traffic Forecasting
children.gist: Road networks modeled as graphs support estimated-time-of-arrival prediction, a problem essential to both navigation apps and businesses like delivery or ride-sharing that depend on accurate travel-time estimates.

children.title: Graph Neural Networks for ETA
children.gist: Graph neural networks now predict estimated arrival times directly as a graph regression task, deployed in production by Google Maps and Baidu Maps using spatio-temporal attention models.

children.title: Object Recognition
children.gist: Convolutional neural networks achieved breakthroughs on ImageNet classification and object detection, with architectures like AlexNet, VGG-16, and ResNets surpassing human performance and enabling tasks from captioning to autonomous driving.

children.title: Game Playing
children.gist: CNN-based reinforcement learning agents, from AlphaGo to MuZero and Agent57, achieved superhuman performance in Go, chess, Shogi, and dozens of Atari games by extracting features from grid-like game states.

children.title: Text and Speech Synthesis
children.gist: One-dimensional grid data like text and speech have been transformed by dilated convolutions in WaveNet, and then by Transformers like BERT and GPT-3, which generate remarkably human-like language and speech.

children.title: Healthcare
children.gist: Geometric Deep Learning aids medicine through grid-based imaging diagnosis, mesh models of organs like the brain, functional brain networks for disease prediction, and patient graphs built from demographic or health-record similarity.

children.title: Particle Physics and Astrophysics
children.gist: Particle physics and astrophysics data, naturally unordered sets of interacting particles, are now modeled as graphs for jet classification, neutrino detection, and analysis of cosmic microwave background radiation.

children.title: Virtual and Augmented Reality
children.gist: Mesh convolutional networks and geometric autoencoders model 3D body, face, and hand shapes for motion capture and synthesis, powering real-time augmented reality products such as those acquired by Snap.

children.title: Historic Perspective
children.gist: Symmetry's role as an organizing idea runs from ancient geometry through Klein, Noether, and gauge physics, into decades of machine learning work that independently converged on the same invariance principles now named Geometric Deep Learning.
children.question: Symmetry's history — how did independent threads in mathematics, physics, and machine learning converge on today's geometric deep learning? (a historical trace across fields)

children.title: Ancient Roots of Symmetry
children.gist: Hermann Weyl's reflections on symmetry trace the idea from Sumerian and Pythagorean designs through Plato's five regular solids to Kepler's explanation of snowflakes' six-fold shape as hexagonal particle packing.

children.title: Symmetry in Mathematics and Physics
children.gist: Group theory, developed by Galois, Lie, and Klein's Erlangen Program, became mathematics' language for symmetry, while Noether showed symmetries yield conservation laws and gauge invariance later unified the fundamental forces.

children.title: Early Use of Symmetry in Machine Learning
children.gist: Before deep learning, researchers built equivariant pattern detectors and proved limits on single-layer perceptrons, motivating multi-layer networks, while Neocognitron and later convolutional networks built shift invariance directly into their architecture.
children.sourceHeading: Early Use of Symmetry in Machine Learning

children.title: Graph Neural Networks
children.gist: Graph neural networks emerged gradually from 1990s recursive models over tree structures, through the first generic formulations by Gori and Scarselli using recurrent fixed-point computation, later simplified by gated architectures.

children.title: Computational Chemistry
children.gist: Independently of mainstream graph neural network research, computational chemists since the 1990s modeled molecules as graphs of atoms and bonds, producing early architectures that anticipated modern designs and now drive drug screening.

children.title: Node Embeddings
children.gist: Early unsupervised graph representation learning relied on random-walk embeddings like DeepWalk and node2vec, later shown equivalent to matrix factorization, before researchers shifted toward contrastive, mutual-information-based self-supervised objectives.

children.title: Probabilistic Graphical Models
children.gist: Graph neural networks independently resurfaced by embedding probabilistic graphical model computations, with structure2vec linking mean-field inference and belief propagation to message passing, inspiring combinations with conditional random fields and Markov networks.

children.title: The Weisfeiler-Lehman Formalism
children.gist: Researchers discovered that graph neural networks' expressive power is bounded by the classical Weisfeiler-Lehman graph isomorphism test, motivating injective aggregation like summation and architectures such as the Graph Isomorphism Network.

children.title: Higher-order Methods
children.gist: To exceed Weisfeiler-Lehman's limits, researchers built higher-order k-GNNs operating on node tuples, proved equivalences to k-WL tests, and devised structural augmentations like node identifiers to detect substructures such as rings.

children.title: Signal Processing and Harmonic Analysis
children.gist: Drawing on harmonic analysis and computational neuroscience, researchers built theoretical frameworks like M-theory, steerable pyramids, and scattering transforms to explain why convolutional neural networks work via multiscale wavelet decompositions.

children.title: Signal Processing on Graphs and Meshes
children.gist: Spectral graph neural networks grew from Graph Signal Processing, which generalized Fourier transforms to graph Laplacian eigenvectors, building on even earlier spectral techniques from computer graphics for mesh and shape analysis.
children.sourceHeading: Signal Processing on Graph and Meshes

children.title: Computer Graphics and Geometry Processing
children.gist: Geometry processing researchers built intrinsic metric-invariant shape models and the first mesh convolutional networks, later generalized through attention-based architectures, while parallel point-cloud and graph-learning work enabled latent graph learning and Transformers.

children.title: Algorithmic Reasoning
children.gist: Neural networks can be designed to mimic algorithms' invariant computational structure, aligning with dynamic programming, learning primitive operations, and extrapolating to new input sizes by preserving algorithms' preconditions and postconditions.

children.title: Geometric Deep Learning
children.gist: The term Geometric Deep Learning originated in a 2015 grant and a 2017 paper, was later reframed by Max Welling's grids-graphs-groups-gauges scheme, to which this text adds geodesics as a fifth domain.
